Argument for “Beggarhood as Viable Strategy with Tangible Benefits”

I maintain that Skkiru’s embrace of beggar status is neither a hopeless imposition nor merely a temporary endurance test, but a deliberate, resourceful strategy yielding essential material, social, and strategic advantages—and positioning him for ultimate restoration. Debater_B’s “unsustainable fallacy” overlooks Skkiru’s repeated agency, the very structure of the plan, and his own choice to persist.  

I. Beggarhood Provides Crucial, Irreplaceable Resources  
1. Life-Saving Imports: Skkiru must “eat the candy … then and there” precisely because “Chocolate was found only in the most expensive of the planet’s delicacy shops—and now neither delicacy shops nor chocolate were to be found” (p. XX).  
   - He would die without Terran gifts; “Chocolate increased the body’s resistance to weather” (p. XX). This direct survival benefit validates the beggar role.  
   - If Bbulas truly intended gifts for his Treasury, he would bar Skkiru’s access—but he doesn’t: “Hurry up, Skkiru … They mustn’t suspect the existence of the city underground or we’re finished” (p. XX). Only beggars can approach the ship without betraying the secret.  

2. Authenticity to Attract Earthmen: The entire plan “requires us to be different … primitive societies … to attract Earthmen” (p. XX).  
   - His rags and muddy sandals lend credibility: “If they stand out here in the cold much longer, they are going to turn bright yellow” (p. XX). The rain dance and mud convey primitive allure, essential to keep Earthmen engaged.  
   - Earthmen comment on the “attractive mud” (p. XX), “Such texture, such scent” (p. XX), proving the primitive appearance works.

II. Beggar Role Grants Strategic Mobility and Discretion  
1. Preemptive Access: Skkiru uses salvaged land gear “while Bbulas was looking the other way… he was at the Earth ship long before the official greeters” (p. XX).  
   - He leverages “most primitive” guise to advance his own ends—he isn’t trapped but covertly mobile, gathering data, resources, and rapport.  
   - This would be impossible from the priestly class, constrained by ceremony. Beggarhood thus expands his tactical options.

2. Opportunity for Innovation: Skkiru’s willingness to try new methods (“idea from an old sporting fictape … equipment … salvaged from a wrecked air-car” [p. XX]) demonstrates resourcefulness.  
   - He “hoped it wouldn’t reach his antennae” (p. XX), yet acts boldly—showing psychological flexibility and drive to succeed.

III. Psychological and Romantic Potential  
1. Primitive Romance Trope: Skkiru intends “to make something of himself and show that a beggar was worthy of the high priestess’s hand—which would be entirely in the Terran primitive tradition of romance” (p. XX).  
   - He “could not reconcile himself … but as a patriotic citizen, he would abide by it” (p. XX) and “hunt sympathy in ritual … and make his fortune” (implied). Primitive romances often celebrate the rise of the outcast.  

2. Persistence Indicates Viability: Despite discomfort, he “answers sulkily… ‘I don't have to like doing it, and I don't intend to like doing it’ … yet he complies” (p. XX).  
   - If beggarhood were truly hopeless, he would retreat or starve. Instead, he persists, exploits it (chocolate), and “regardless of personal misery…“he hoped” for Larhgan’s occasional kisses on feast days” (p. XX), implying psychological reward.

IV. Debater_B’s “Unsustainable” Thesis Falls Short  
1. Reliance on Earthmen is by Design: The plan hinges on the East–West dynamic; “we must not establish undue rapport… find out later” (p. XX) shows cautious but ongoing engagement. The “temporary” nature is under Bbulas’ control, not Skkiru’s.  
2. Suffering as Proof of Authenticity: The “rags” and “wind and rain” aren’t evidence of failure but part of the theatrical authenticity essential to lure further imports and continued visits.  
3. Mobility and Secret Underground Cities: Skkiru “could emigrate” but refuses “not playing the game” (p. XX). His commitment suggests belief in eventual success; he stays to “see Larhgan” and “fulfill the mission.”  

Conclusion  
Skkiru’s beggarhood is a calculated, reversible stage in a covert cultural performance, yielding indispensable resources (chocolate), strategic mobility, and narrative potential for romance and restoration. His own agency, repeated exploitation of advantages, and persistence demonstrate he regards it not as an unsustainable fallacy but as a essential, effective role paving the way for planetary salvation—and his personal vindication. Debater_B’s misery-centric reading neglects the plan’s core mechanisms and Skkiru’s unwavering strategic use of beggar status.
